subject: math
title: Ratios, Rates, Proportions, and Percents
objectives: You will write and simplify ratios and use a ratio to split a total into parts.
You will find unit rates and unit prices, compare deals, and solve distance-rate-time problems.
You will set up and solve proportions, including recipe, map-scale, and unit-conversion problems.
You will convert among fractions, decimals, and percents and find a part, a percent, or a whole.
You will calculate percent change, discounts, sales tax, tips, and simple interest, including multi-step problems.

slides.title: Week 2 Math: Ratios, Rates, and Percents
slides.board:
Ratios, Rates, Proportions, and Percents

  • Write and simplify ratios; split a total using a ratio
  • Find unit rates and unit prices; compare deals
  • Set up and solve proportions
  • Convert fractions, decimals, and percents; find a part, a percent, or a whole
  • Percent change, discounts, tax, tips, and simple interest

Today: warm-up, ratios and rates, proportions, percents, percent change, interest, GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 2. This week is about comparing numbers: how many of one thing for each of another, how fast, how much per ounce, and what percent. You already do this every time you check a shelf tag, double a recipe, figure a tip, or look at a loan offer. Today we put names and reliable methods to what you already do, so that the GED's trap answers stop working on you. Same rhythm as last week: I explain, I show a worked example, we do some together, then you try some on your own.
ask: Where did you last use a percent or a rate in real life: a sale, a tip, a paycheck, gas mileage? (expected answer: any; use their example later in the lesson)
notes.watch: Pacing for 60 minutes: warm-up 5 min (slide 2); ratios and rates 12 min (slides 3–8); proportions 10 min (slides 9–12); percents 8 min (slides 13–15); discounts and percent change 12 min (slides 16–20); simple interest 6 min (slides 21–23); GED questions, strategy, recap 7 min (slides 24–27). If you fall behind, cut the we-do slides to two problems each.

slides.title: Warm-up: Week 1 Review
slides.board:
Work these on paper. No calculator.

  1. Simplify 18/24.
  2. Write 3/8 as a decimal.
  3. 2.4 × 0.05
  4. 7.2 ÷ 0.6
  5. 20 − 12 ÷ 4 × 2
steps: 3. 24 × 5 = 120; three decimal places in all, so 0.12 (0.120)

notes.say: These five come straight from last week, and every one of them shows up again today. Simplifying a fraction is how you simplify a ratio. Fraction to decimal is how you turn a fraction into a percent. Decimal multiplication and division are how you find a percent of a number and a unit price. Take about three minutes, then tell me your answers one at a time.
ask: How did you get 3/8 as a decimal? (expected answer: divide 3 by 8)
On number 5, what did you do first? (expected answer: 12 ÷ 4, because division comes before subtraction)
notes.watch: Number 3: 1.2 or 0.012 means the decimal places were not counted (there are three: one in 2.4 and two in 0.05). Number 4: 1.2 means only one decimal point was moved. Number 5: 4 means the student subtracted first, (20 − 12) ÷ 4 × 2; 18.5 means they multiplied 4 × 2 before dividing. Fix these now; they come back in every percent problem today.

slides.title: Ratios: Part to Part and Part to Whole
slides.board:
A ratio compares two quantities: 3 to 5, 3:5, or 3/5. Order matches the words.

A tray has 5 red tiles and 3 blue tilesRatio
red to blue (part to part)5:3
blue to red (part to part)3:5
red to all tiles (part to whole)5:8
  • Simplify like a fraction: 36:48 = 3:4 (divide both by 12).
  • A ratio a:b has a + b parts in all.

notes.say: A ratio is a comparison, and the order of the words tells you the order of the numbers. Red to blue is 5 to 3; blue to red is 3 to 5, and those are different statements. The most important idea on this slide is the last line. A ratio like 5 to 3 is about parts. If you want the whole, you add the parts: 5 plus 3 is 8. So red is 5 out of 8 tiles, not 5 out of 3. The GED loves to ask for the part-to-whole fraction when you are given a part-to-part ratio.
ask: A class has 15 women and 10 men. What is the ratio of men to women in simplest form? (expected answer: 2:3)
In that class, what fraction of the students are women? (expected answer: 15/25 = 3/5)
notes.watch: The classic error is saying that with a 3:5 ratio, the first quantity is 3/5 of the total. Draw 8 boxes and shade 3: it is 3/8. Also watch for reversed order on “men to women.”

slides.title: Split a Total Using a Ratio
slides.board:
A community garden will plant tomatoes and peppers in a ratio of 5:3. There is room for 72 plants. How many of each should be planted?

Method: add the parts → divide the total by the parts → multiply.

notes.say: Here is the method for splitting a total. Think of the ratio as a recipe of parts: 5 parts tomatoes and 3 parts peppers makes 8 equal parts. The 72 plants fill those 8 parts, so each part is 9 plants. Then multiply each side of the ratio by 9. Always check two ways: the pieces add back to the total, and they simplify back to the ratio.
ask: Why do we divide 72 by 8 and not by 5? (expected answer: there are 8 parts in all; 72 is the total, not the tomatoes)
notes.watch: A student who divides 72 by 5 or by 3 is treating the total as one of the parts. Ask, “Is 72 the tomatoes, the peppers, or everything?”

slides.title: Ratios Together
slides.board:
1. Simplify 36:48.
  2. A team won 18 games and lost 12. What is the ratio of wins to games played?
  3. The ratio of women to men in a class of 28 is 3:4. How many women are in the class?
  4. A paint color mixes blue and white in a ratio of 2:7. How many quarts of white go with 4 quarts of blue?
steps: 2. Games played = 18 + 12 = 30. Wins to games played = 18:30 = 3:5
4. Blue went from 2 to 4, so multiply both by 2: 2:7 = 4:14, so 14 quarts of white

notes.say: Let's do these together. Before you compute, tell me whether the question wants part to part or part to whole. Number 2 is the trap: the question says games played, which is the whole. Number 4 is a preview of proportions: when one side of a ratio is scaled up, the other side scales by the same factor.
ask: In number 2, what is the whole? (expected answer: 30 games played)
In number 4, what did we multiply by? (expected answer: 2, because 2 quarts of blue became 4)
notes.watch: Number 2: 3:2 means the student wrote wins to losses. Number 3: 16 is the number of men. Number 4: 9 quarts means the student added 2 to each side (2 + 2 = 4, 7 + 2 = 9); ratios scale by multiplying, not adding.

slides.title: Rates and Unit Rates
slides.board:
A rate compares different units. A unit rate is the amount for 1 unit. Divide to find it.

RateDivideUnit rate
135 miles in 3 hours135 ÷ 345 miles per hour
$391 for 23 hours391 ÷ 23$17 per hour
$6.45 for 5 pounds6.45 ÷ 5$1.29 per pound

Unit price = price ÷ units. Lower unit price = better buy. d = rt (on the formula sheet).

notes.say: A rate is a ratio with two different kinds of units, like miles and hours or dollars and pounds. The unit rate tells you how much for one. The word “per” is your signal: dollars per pound means dollars divided by pounds, in that order. When you compare two sizes of the same product, the shelf price does not tell you the better deal; the unit price does. And the distance formula, distance equals rate times time, is on your GED formula sheet, so you can find any one of the three if you know the other two.
ask: Four pounds of grapes cost $3.60. What is the price per pound? (expected answer: $0.90)
A car goes 50 miles per hour for 3 hours. How far does it go? (expected answer: 150 miles, d = rt)
notes.watch: Students divide the wrong way: 5 ÷ 6.45 gives about 0.78, which is pounds per dollar, not dollars per pound. Have them say the units out loud: “dollars per pound” means dollars on top.

slides.title: Which Is the Better Buy?
slides.board:
The same laundry detergent comes in two sizes.

64 ounces$9.92
100 ounces$14.50

Which is the better buy?
steps: The 100-ounce bottle is the better buy, by about one cent per ounce.

notes.say: The 64-ounce bottle has the lower price on the shelf, but it is a smaller bottle, so that comparison is not fair. To compare fairly, find what one ounce costs in each bottle. Divide dollars by ounces for each one, then compare. Keep three decimal places when the unit prices are close; rounding too early can make two different prices look the same.
ask: What would you do if one item was priced per pound and the other per ounce? (expected answer: convert so both use the same unit first; 1 pound = 16 ounces)
notes.watch: Watch for a student who picks the cheaper bottle by shelf price. Ask, “How much do you get for that price?” Also, the bigger size is not automatically the better buy; you have to compute.

slides.title: Your Turn: Ratios and Rates
slides.board:
Three minutes. Work on paper, then tell me your answers.

  1. Simplify 45:60.
  2. A shelter has only dogs and cats, 63 animals in all. The ratio of dogs to cats is 4:5. How many cats?
  3. A printer prints 192 pages in 8 minutes. How many pages per minute?
  4. A 12-pack of water costs $4.68. A 24-pack costs $8.88. Which is the better buy?

notes.say: Your turn. I am starting the clock for three minutes. For each one, write the method you used in a few words next to the answer: simplify, split, unit rate, or compare unit prices. When time is up, read me your four answers.
ask: Read me your four answers. (expected answer: 3:4; 35; 24; the 24-pack)
notes.answer: (1) GCF 15: 45:60 = 3:4   (2) 4 + 5 = 9 parts; 63 ÷ 9 = 7; cats = 5 × 7 = 35   (3) 192 ÷ 8 = 24   (4) $4.68 ÷ 12 = $0.39 per bottle; $8.88 ÷ 24 = $0.37 per bottle, so the 24-pack
notes.watch: Number 2: 28 is the number of dogs; 78.75 means the student divided 63 by 4 and multiplied by 5 (treating 63 as the dogs). Number 4: choosing the 12-pack because $4.68 is less than $8.88 is the shelf-price trap.

slides.title: Proportions and Cross Products
slides.board:
A proportion says two ratios are equal: 2/3 = 8/12.

Cross products: if a/b = c/d, then a × d = b × c.   Check: 2 × 12 = 24 and 3 × 8 = 24.

  1. Write unit labels first: cups/servings = cups/servings
  2. Fill in numbers; use x for the unknown.
  3. Cross multiply.
  4. Divide to get x alone.
  5. Sense check: bigger situation, bigger answer?

notes.say: Use a proportion whenever something scales up or down at a steady rate: a recipe, a map, a medicine dose, a unit conversion. The math is easy; the setup is where people lose points. So before you write a single number, write the labels: cups over servings equals cups over servings. If the top of the left side is cups, the top of the right side must be cups too. Then cross multiply, divide, and ask yourself whether the size of the answer makes sense.
ask: Solve x/4 = 6/8. (expected answer: 8x = 24, so x = 3)
If a/b = c/d, what are the two cross products? (expected answer: a × d and b × c)
notes.watch: The most common setup error is flipping one side: cups/servings = servings/cups. It produces an answer that is far too big or far too small, which is why the sense check matters.

slides.title: Map Scale
slides.board: On a state map, 1/2 inch represents 12 miles. Two cities are 3 3/4 inches apart on the map. What is the actual distance between them?
steps: Sense check: 1 inch is 24 miles, and 3.75 inches is a little less than 4 inches, so a little less than 96 miles. 90 fits.

notes.say: Map scale is a proportion problem. Change the fractions to decimals so the arithmetic is easy: one half is 0.5 and three and three fourths is 3.75. Put inches on top on both sides and miles on the bottom on both sides. Then cross multiply. My favorite sense check here is to find what 1 inch stands for: if half an inch is 12 miles, a full inch is 24 miles.
ask: What does 1 inch represent on this map? (expected answer: 24 miles)
notes.watch: If a student gets about 0.16, they set it up as 0.5/12 = x/3.75 (inches over miles on the left, miles over inches on the right). An answer of 1,440 or more means a number was multiplied instead of divided. Point to the labels and ask whether 3.75 inches should be more or less than 12 miles.

slides.title: Proportions Together
slides.board:
1. Solve: x/8 = 15/24
  2. A rice recipe for 6 servings uses 1 1/2 cups of rice. How much rice is needed for 10 servings?
  3. A car goes 168 miles on 6 gallons of gas. At that rate, how far can it go on 10 gallons?
  4. There are 3 feet in 1 yard. How many yards are in 42 feet?
steps: 3. 168/6 = x/10 → 6x = 1,680 → x = 280 miles (or: 168 ÷ 6 = 28 miles per gallon, × 10)

notes.say: Let's set these up together. For each word problem, tell me the labels before you tell me the numbers. Notice number 3 can be solved two ways: as a proportion or by finding the unit rate first. Both are correct; use whichever feels natural. Number 4 shows that unit conversions are proportions too.
ask: What labels did you use in number 2? (expected answer: cups/servings = cups/servings)
In number 3, what is the unit rate? (expected answer: 28 miles per gallon)
notes.watch: Number 2: 5.5 cups means the student saw the servings go up by 4 and added 4 cups (additive thinking). Number 4: 126 means they multiplied 42 × 3 instead of dividing; ask whether there should be more yards or fewer yards than feet.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Proportions
slides.board:
A medicine dose is 15 milligrams for every 20 pounds of body weight. How many milligrams should a patient who weighs 164 pounds receive?

A. 159 mg    B. 123 mg    C. 218.7 mg    D. 2,460 mg
steps: Eliminate A (159 mg): it comes from adding: the weight went up 144 pounds (164 − 20), so someone adds 144 to 15. Doses scale by multiplying, not adding.
Eliminate C (218.7 mg): it comes from a flipped setup, 15/20 = 164/x (mg/pounds = pounds/mg), which gives 20 × 164 ÷ 15. Keep the labels in the same positions.
Eliminate D (2,460 mg): it is 15 × 164, the cross product, before dividing by 20. The last step is missing.
B (123 mg) is correct: 15/20 = x/164; 20x = 15 × 164 = 2,460; x = 2,460 ÷ 20 = 123. Check: 0.75 mg per pound × 164 = 123.

notes.say: Here is a GED-style proportion with real-world stakes. Every wrong answer comes from a mistake we have talked about: adding instead of scaling, flipping one side of the proportion, and stopping one step early. Solve it first, then use the other choices as a checklist of traps.
ask: Which choice did you get, and what was your setup? (expected answer: B, 123 mg; mg/pounds = mg/pounds, 15/20 = x/164)
notes.watch: If the student picked D, they did the hard part and skipped the easy part. Have them reread their last line and ask, “Is x alone yet?”

slides.title: Percents: Part, Percent, Whole
slides.board:
Percent means “out of 100.” 35% = 35/100 = 0.35.

  • Percent → decimal: point 2 places left (7% = 0.07; 125% = 1.25)
  • Decimal → percent: point 2 places right (0.6 = 60%)
  • Fraction → percent: divide, then move (3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%)

part = percent × whole   or   part/whole = percent/100

Find the partWhat is 15% of 60?
Find the percent27 is what percent of 36?
Find the whole18 is 40% of what number?

notes.say: Percent just means out of 100, so every percent is a fraction with 100 on the bottom. To use a percent in a calculation, change it to a decimal by moving the point two places left. Then nearly every percent question uses one relationship: part equals percent times whole. There are only three versions, depending on which piece is missing. In word problems, “of” usually points to the whole and “is” usually points to the part.
ask: Write 6% as a decimal. (expected answer: 0.06)
What is 10% of 70? What is 5% of 70? (expected answer: 7; 3.5)
notes.watch: 6% written as 0.6 is the most expensive mistake on this page; it makes every answer ten times too big. Insist on two places: the point starts after the 6 and moves two places left, so 6% = 0.06.

slides.title: The Three Percent Questions
slides.board:
(a) What is 15% of 60?

(b) 27 is what percent of 36?

(c) 18 is 40% of what number?

Use part = percent × whole each time.
steps: (b) Find the percent: 27 = percent × 36, so percent = 27 ÷ 36 = 0.75 = 75%
(c) Find the whole: 18 = 0.40 × whole, so whole = 18 ÷ 0.40 = 45

notes.say: Same equation three times. When the part is missing, multiply. When the percent or the whole is missing, divide the part by the other number. Here is a sense check for finding the whole: if 18 is only 40 percent of the number, the number must be bigger than 18. If you get an answer smaller than the part, you multiplied when you should have divided.
ask: In (c), why must the answer be bigger than 18? (expected answer: 18 is only part of it, less than half)
notes.watch: On (c), 7.2 means the student multiplied 0.40 × 18. On (b), 133% means they divided 36 ÷ 27, whole over part.

slides.title: Your Turn: Proportions and Percents
slides.board:
Three minutes.

  1. Solve: 4/10 = x/35
  2. On a floor plan, 1 inch represents 8 feet. A room is 2.5 inches long on the plan. How long is the actual room?
  3. What is 8% of 350?
  4. 12 is 30% of what number?

notes.say: Your turn again. Three minutes on the clock. For the two percent problems, write the equation part equals percent times whole and put in what you know before you calculate.
ask: Read me your four answers. (expected answer: 14; 20 feet; 28; 40)
notes.watch: Number 3: 280 means 8% was used as 0.8. Number 4: 3.6 means the student multiplied 0.30 × 12; the whole must be bigger than 12.

slides.title: Discounts, Sales Tax, and Tips
slides.board:
SituationLong wayShortcut
30% offprice − 0.30 × priceprice × 0.70
6% sales taxprice + 0.06 × priceprice × 1.06
20% tipbill + 0.20 × billbill × 1.20

Mental math: 10% = move the point 1 place left. 5% = half of 10%. 15% = 10% + 5%.

Do each percent in order, on the price at that moment.

notes.say: A discount comes off the price; tax and tips are added to it. You can find the amount and then subtract or add, or you can use the shortcut: 30 percent off means you still pay 70 percent, so multiply by 0.70. Six percent tax means you pay 106 percent, so multiply by 1.06. For tips, build from 10 percent in your head: on a $46 bill, 10 percent is $4.60, 5 percent is $2.30, so 15 percent is $6.90. When there are several percents in a row, do them one at a time, each on the new price.
ask: What do you multiply by for 25% off? For 8% tax? (expected answer: 0.75; 1.08)
What is a 15% tip on $60, in your head? (expected answer: $6 + $3 = $9)
notes.watch: Students who multiply by 0.30 for “30% off” get the discount, not the sale price. Ask, “Is your answer what you save or what you pay?”

slides.title: Discount, Then Tax
slides.board: A jacket regularly costs $85. It is on sale for 30% off. Sales tax of 6% is charged on the sale price. What is the total cost?

notes.say: Two percents, one after the other. First the discount, which gives the sale price. Then tax on the sale price, not on the original price. I will show both the long way and the shortcut; on the calculator part of the GED the shortcut is faster and has fewer places to slip. Before calculating, estimate: about $85 minus about $25 is about $60, plus a few dollars of tax, so the answer should be a little over $60.
ask: What would you get if you took tax on the original $85 instead? (expected answer: $59.50 + $5.10 = $64.60, which is wrong)
notes.watch: Some students subtract 30% and add 6% as one step, 24% off: $85 × 0.76 = $64.60. It is close but wrong, and the GED puts exactly that number in the choices.

slides.title: Percent Change
slides.board:
Percent change = (new − original) ÷ original, then write it as a percent.

  • Always divide by the original (starting) value.
  • Positive = increase; negative = decrease.
  • Up 20% then down 20% is not back to start: $100 → $120 → $96.
  • Working backward: after 25% off, the sale price is 75% of the original, so original = sale price ÷ 0.75.

notes.say: Percent change measures a change against where you started. Find the change, then divide by the original value, never the new one. That one rule is behind most of the trap answers on this topic. Two more ideas: a percent increase followed by the same percent decrease does not cancel out, because the second percent is taken from a different number. And when you know the price after a discount and want the original, divide by what percent you paid; do not add the percent back on.
ask: A price goes from $50 to $60. What is the percent increase? (expected answer: 10 ÷ 50 = 20%)
A price goes from $60 back to $50. Is that a 20% decrease? (expected answer: no; 10 ÷ 60 ≈ 16.7%)
notes.watch: If a student says the second question is also 20%, ask, “What is the original now?” It is $60, so the base changed.

slides.title: Percent Increase: Rent
slides.board: A family's rent went from $1,150 to $1,265 per month. What was the percent increase?
steps: Trap: 115 ÷ 1,265 ≈ 0.091, or about 9.1%. That divides by the new rent, and it often appears as a choice.

notes.say: Three steps: find the change, divide by the original, write it as a percent. The original here is the old rent, $1,150. Watch the last line. If you divide by the new rent, you get about 9.1 percent, which looks reasonable and is wrong. The GED will offer it.
ask: Which number is the original, and how do you know? (expected answer: $1,150, the rent before the change)
notes.watch: Ask the student to circle the original value in the problem before doing any math. That habit prevents the 9.1% trap.

slides.title: Percent Problems Together
slides.board:
1. A dinner bill is $46.00. You leave an 18% tip. What is the total?
  2. A phone's price dropped from $640 to $544. What was the percent decrease?
  3. A $100 item goes up 20%, then the new price goes down 20%. What is the final price?
  4. A $120 item is 20% off, then an extra 10% off the sale price. What is the final price?

notes.say: Let's work these together. Numbers 3 and 4 are about percents in a row. Each new percent is taken from the price at that moment, so the percents do not simply add or cancel. Tell me the multiplier you will use for each step before you compute.
ask: What multiplier do you use for each step in number 4? (expected answer: 0.80, then 0.90)
In number 2, what do you divide by? (expected answer: 640, the original price)
notes.watch: Number 2: about 17.6% means dividing by the new price, 544. Number 3: $100 means the student assumed the percents cancel. Number 4: $84 means 30% off in one step ($120 × 0.70).

slides.title: Simple Interest
slides.board:
I = Prt   (on the GED formula sheet)

Iinterest (the extra money)
Pprincipal: amount borrowed or saved
ryearly rate, as a decimal (4.5% = 0.045)
ttime in years (18 months = 1.5 years)

Total paid back or account balance = P + I.

notes.say: When you borrow or save, interest is the price of using the money. Simple interest uses one formula, I equals P r t, and it is printed on your formula sheet. What the sheet does not tell you is the two rules that cost people points. The rate is per year, so time must be in years: divide months by 12. And interest is only the extra money; if the question asks for the total paid back or the balance in the account, add the principal.
ask: Write 30 months in years. (expected answer: 2.5 years)
Simple interest on $800 at 5% for 2 years? (expected answer: 800 × 0.05 × 2 = $80)
notes.watch: A student who uses t = 30 for 30 months will get an interest amount larger than the loan. Teach them to sanity-check: a few percent a year for a few years should be a small fraction of P.

slides.title: A Simple-Interest Loan
slides.board: Andre borrows $2,400 at 4.5% simple interest per year for 3 years. How much interest does he pay, and what is the total he pays back?

notes.say: Find one year of interest first; it makes the arithmetic easier to check. One year is $108, so three years is $324. That is the interest. The total Andre pays back is the loan plus the interest. On the GED, both $324 and $2,724 will be choices, and only one of them answers the question that was asked.
ask: If the loan were for 6 months instead, what would t be? (expected answer: 0.5)
notes.watch: Watch the decimal: 4.5% is 0.045, not 0.45. Using 0.45 gives $3,240 in interest, more than the loan itself.

slides.title: Your Turn: Percent Change and Interest
slides.board:
Four minutes.

  1. A town grew from 8,000 to 9,200 people. Percent increase?
  2. Boots were marked down from $50 to $42. Percent decrease?
  3. Simple interest on $1,500 at 6% per year for 8 months?
  4. Luis saves $5,000 at 2.5% simple interest per year. How much is in the account after 4 years?

notes.say: Last independent round. Four minutes. On the interest problems, write t in years before you do anything else, and underline what the question asks for: the interest or the total.
ask: Read me your four answers. (expected answer: 15%, 16%, $60, $5,500)
notes.watch: Number 1: about 13% means dividing by 9,200. Number 3: $720 means t = 8 was used. Number 4: $500 is only the interest.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Working Backward
slides.board:
After a 25% discount, a coat costs $66. What was the original price of the coat?

A. $82.50    B. $49.50    C. $88.00    D. $16.50
steps: Eliminate D ($16.50): that is 25% of $66 (0.25 × 66). It is a discount amount, and of the wrong price.
Eliminate B ($49.50): that takes another 25% off the sale price ($66 × 0.75). The original must be more than $66.
Eliminate A ($82.50): that adds 25% of $66 back on ($66 × 1.25). The 25% was taken from the original price, not from $66. Check: 25% off $82.50 is $61.88, not $66.
C ($88.00) is correct: the sale price is 75% of the original, so 0.75 × original = 66 and original = 66 ÷ 0.75 = $88. Check: 25% of $88 is $22, and $88 − $22 = $66.

notes.say: This is one of the most-missed percent questions, because the natural move, adding 25 percent back, is wrong. Ask yourself: 25 percent of what? It was 25 percent of the original price. So the $66 is the 75 percent that was left. Set up 0.75 times the original equals 66 and divide. And always check by running the discount forward.
ask: Which choice did you pick, and how did you check it? (expected answer: C, $88; 25% of $88 is $22, and $88 − $22 = $66)
notes.watch: If the student picked A, have them check it forward: 25% off $82.50 is $61.88. Seeing the check fail is more convincing than any rule.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Simple Interest
slides.board:
Marisol borrows $4,000 at 6% simple interest per year for 18 months. What is the total amount she pays back?

A. $360    B. $4,240    C. $4,360    D. $8,320
steps: Eliminate D ($8,320): it uses t = 18 (months) in I = Prt: 4,000 × 0.06 × 18 = 4,320, plus 4,000. Time must be in years.
Eliminate A ($360): that is the interest only. The question asks for the total she pays back.
Eliminate B ($4,240): it uses only 1 year of interest ($240) and drops the extra 6 months.
C ($4,360) is correct: t = 18 ÷ 12 = 1.5 years; I = 4,000 × 0.06 × 1.5 = $360; total = $4,000 + $360 = $4,360.

notes.say: Formula-sheet questions test whether you know what the letters mean. The formula is given; the traps are the time unit and the question being asked. Underline “18 months” and “total amount” before you start.
ask: What is t, and what does the question ask for? (expected answer: t = 1.5 years; the total, P + I)
notes.watch: Students who choose A did all the math correctly and then answered a different question. Make rereading the last sentence a habit.

slides.title: GED Strategy: Estimate, Then Reread the Question

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
This week is about comparing numbers: how many of one thing for each of another, how fast, how much per ounce, and what percent. You already use these skills when you check a price tag, double a recipe, read a map, figure a tip, or look at a loan offer. This lesson gives you reliable methods so the GED's trap answers stop working on you.

By the end, you will be able to:

  • Write and simplify ratios, and use a ratio to split a total into parts.
  • Find unit rates and unit prices, compare deals, and use d = rt.
  • Set up and solve proportions for recipes, maps, and conversions.
  • Convert among fractions, decimals, and percents, and find a part, a percent, or a whole.
  • Calculate percent change, discounts, sales tax, tips, and simple interest.

Work one screen at a time and answer each check before you move on. Keep paper, a pencil, and a calculator nearby; try the first few screens by hand.

screens.title: Writing and Simplifying Ratios
screens.html:
A ratio compares two quantities. The ratio of 12 nurses to 4 doctors can be written three ways: 12 to 4, 12:4, or 12/4.

Order matters. Write the numbers in the same order as the words. “Nurses to doctors” is 12:4, but “doctors to nurses” is 4:12.

Simplify a ratio the same way you simplify a fraction: divide both numbers by their greatest common factor (GCF). 12:4 becomes 3:1 when you divide both by 4. That means there are 3 nurses for every 1 doctor.

If you are not sure of the GCF, divide by any common factor and keep going until no number except 1 divides both.

example.prompt: A community center has 36 adult volunteers and 48 youth players. Write the ratio of volunteers to players in simplest form.
steps: Write in the order of the words: volunteers to players = 36:48.
The GCF of 36 and 48 is 12. 36 ÷ 12 = 3 and 48 ÷ 12 = 4.

check.prompt: A bread recipe uses 12 cups of flour and 8 cups of water. Write the ratio of flour to water in simplest form. Type it like 5:2.

mistakes.why: That is water to flour. The question asks for flour to water, so flour (12) comes first: 12:8 = 3:2.
6:4 is equal to 12:8, but it is not in simplest form. 6 and 4 can both still be divided by 2: 3:2.

check.hint: Write the numbers in the order of the words. Then divide both by the greatest common factor.
check.explain:
Flour to water = 12:8.

The GCF of 12 and 8 is 4: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and 8 ÷ 4 = 2.

The ratio is 3:2.

If you wrote 2:3, you reversed the order; the words say flour first.

screens.title: Part to Part, Part to Whole
screens.html:
A ratio can compare a part to another part, or a part to the whole.

Suppose a tray holds 5 red tiles and 3 blue tiles.

  • Red to blue is 5:3 (part to part).
  • The whole is 5 + 3 = 8 tiles.
  • Red to all tiles is 5:8 (part to whole), so red tiles are 5/8 of the tray.

Key idea: A ratio a:b has a + b parts in all. The first quantity is a/(a + b) of the whole, not a/b.

Many GED questions give a part-to-part ratio and ask about the whole. Always ask yourself: what is the whole here?

example.prompt: A team won 18 games and lost 12. What is the ratio of wins to games played?
steps: Wins to games played = 18:30. Divide both by 6.

check.prompt: In a choir, the ratio of sopranos to altos is 3:5. There are no other singers. What fraction of the choir are sopranos?
why: 3/5 compares sopranos to altos, which is part to part. The whole choir is 3 + 5 = 8 parts, so sopranos are 3/8.
5/8 is the fraction of the choir that are altos. The question asks about sopranos, the 3 in the ratio.
5/3 compares altos to sopranos, part to part and in reverse order. Sopranos are 3 of the 8 parts: 3/8.
check.hint: Add the parts of the ratio to find the whole choir.
check.explain:
The ratio 3:5 means 3 parts sopranos and 5 parts altos, so the whole choir is 3 + 5 = 8 parts.

Sopranos are 3 of the 8 parts: 3/8.

The tempting wrong answer is 3/5, which compares sopranos to altos instead of sopranos to the whole choir.

screens.title: Splitting a Total Using a Ratio
screens.html:
When you know a total and a ratio, you can find each share in three steps.

  1. Add the parts of the ratio to get the number of equal parts.
  2. Divide the total by that number to find the size of one part.
  3. Multiply each number in the ratio by the size of one part.

Check: the shares should add back to the total and simplify back to the ratio.

example.prompt: A salad dressing uses oil and vinegar in a 3:1 ratio. How many tablespoons of oil are in 20 tablespoons of dressing?

check.skill: Splitting a total in a ratio
check.prompt: Two business partners split a profit of $4,500 in a ratio of 2:3. How much does the partner with the larger share receive?

mistakes.why: That is the smaller share (2 × $900). The larger share is 3 parts: 3 × $900 = $2,700.
You divided $4,500 by 2 and multiplied by 3, as if $4,500 were the smaller partner's share. $4,500 is the whole, which is 2 + 3 = 5 parts.
That splits the profit evenly. A 2:3 ratio is not even: there are 5 parts, and the larger share gets 3 of them.

check.hint: How many equal parts are there in all? Find the size of one part first.
check.explain:
Total parts: 2 + 3 = 5.

One part: $4,500 ÷ 5 = $900.

Larger share: 3 × $900 = $2,700. (Smaller share: 2 × $900 = $1,800. Check: $2,700 + $1,800 = $4,500.)

If you got $6,750, you treated $4,500 as the smaller share instead of the total.

screens.title: Rates and Unit Rates
screens.html:
A rate is a ratio that compares two different kinds of units: miles and hours, dollars and hours, pages and minutes.

A unit rate tells how much for one unit of the second quantity. To find it, divide the first quantity by the second.

  • 135 miles in 3 hours: 135 ÷ 3 = 45 miles per hour.
  • 192 pages in 8 minutes: 192 ÷ 8 = 24 pages per minute.

The word per means “divided by.” “Dollars per hour” means dollars ÷ hours, in that order.

Once you know a unit rate, multiply to find any other amount.

example.prompt: Maria earned $391 for working 23 hours. What is her hourly pay? At that rate, how much will she earn for 35 hours?

check.prompt: A machine fills 1,260 bottles in 45 minutes. How many bottles does it fill per minute?

mistakes.why: You multiplied 1,260 × 45. A unit rate is found by dividing: 1,260 bottles ÷ 45 minutes = 28 bottles per minute.
You divided minutes by bottles (45 ÷ 1,260), which gives minutes per bottle. “Bottles per minute” means bottles ÷ minutes.

check.hint: “Bottles per minute” means bottles divided by minutes.
check.explain:
Bottles per minute = bottles ÷ minutes.

1,260 ÷ 45 = 28 bottles per minute.

Check: 28 × 45 = 1,260.

screens.title: Unit Price and the Better Buy
screens.html:
A unit price is the cost of one unit, such as one ounce, one pound, or one item.

unit price = price ÷ number of units

When you compare two sizes of the same product, the one with the lower unit price is the better buy. The shelf price alone does not tell you, because the packages hold different amounts. And the biggest package is not always the best deal; you have to compute.

When unit prices are close, keep three decimal places so you do not round away the difference.

example.prompt: A 64-ounce bottle of detergent costs $9.92. A 100-ounce bottle costs $14.50. Which is the better buy?
example.answer: The 100-ounce bottle is the better buy.

check.prompt: A 16-ounce jar of peanut butter costs $3.52. A 28-ounce jar of the same brand costs $5.88. Which statement is true?
options: The 28-ounce jar is the better buy, at $0.21 per ounce.
The 16-ounce jar is the better buy, at $0.22 per ounce.
The 16-ounce jar is the better buy, because it costs less.
The 28-ounce jar is the better buy, at $4.76 per ounce.
why: $3.52 ÷ 16 = $0.22 per ounce is correct for the small jar, but $0.22 is more than the large jar's $0.21. The lower unit price is the better buy.
You compared shelf prices. The 16-ounce jar costs less because it holds less. Compare the cost of one ounce: $0.22 versus $0.21.
You divided ounces by dollars (28 ÷ 5.88 ≈ 4.76), which is ounces per dollar, not dollars per ounce. The unit price is $5.88 ÷ 28 = $0.21.
check.hint: Divide each price by its number of ounces, then compare.
check.explain:
16-ounce jar: $3.52 ÷ 16 = $0.22 per ounce.

28-ounce jar: $5.88 ÷ 28 = $0.21 per ounce.

$0.21 < $0.22, so the 28-ounce jar is the better buy.

The tempting mistake is choosing the 16-ounce jar because its shelf price is lower.

screens.title: Distance, Rate, and Time
screens.html:
Speed is a rate: distance per unit of time. The GED formula sheet gives the distance formula:

d = rt   distance = rate × time

You can rearrange it to find any piece:

  • Distance: d = r × t
  • Rate: r = d ÷ t
  • Time: t = d ÷ r

Keep the units consistent. If the rate is in miles per hour, the time must be in hours. Change minutes to hours by dividing by 60: 30 minutes = 0.5 hour.

example.prompt: A driver travels at an average speed of 62 miles per hour for 2 hours 30 minutes. How far does she travel?
steps: Change the time to hours: 2 hours 30 minutes = 2.5 hours.

check.prompt: A bus travels at an average speed of 48 miles per hour. How many hours will it take the bus to travel 180 miles?

mistakes.why: You multiplied 48 × 180. To find time, divide distance by rate: t = d ÷ r = 180 ÷ 48 = 3.75 hours.
You divided rate by distance (48 ÷ 180). Time = distance ÷ rate: 180 ÷ 48 = 3.75.
3 hours 45 minutes is correct, but in decimal hours it is 3.75, because 45 minutes is 3/4 of an hour. 3.45 hours would be about 3 hours 27 minutes.

check.hint: Use d = rt and solve for t: t = d ÷ r.

screens.title: Proportions and Cross Products
screens.html:
A proportion is an equation that says two ratios are equal, such as 2/3 = 8/12.

In a proportion, the cross products are equal: if a/b = c/d, then a × d = b × c. Check: 2 × 12 = 24 and 3 × 8 = 24.

To solve a proportion with an unknown:

  1. Cross multiply.
  2. Divide both sides by the number next to x.
  3. Check by putting your answer back in.

mistakes.why: You cross multiplied the wrong pair: 12 × 20 ÷ 15 = 16. The cross products are x × 20 and 12 × 15, so 20x = 180.
You subtracted instead of scaling: 20 is 8 more than 12, so you took 8 from 15. Proportions scale by multiplying. Cross multiply: 20x = 180.

check.hint: Multiply across the equal sign: x × 20 and 12 × 15.
check.explain:
Cross multiply: 20 × x = 12 × 15, so 20x = 180.

Divide by 20: x = 9.

Check: 9/12 = 0.75 and 15/20 = 0.75.

screens.title: Setting Up Proportions in Word Problems
screens.html:
Use a proportion whenever a situation scales up or down at a steady rate: recipes, maps, medicine doses, gas mileage, unit conversions.

  1. Write labels first, such as cups/servings = cups/servings. The same unit must be in the same position on both sides.
  2. Fill in the numbers, using x for the unknown.
  3. Cross multiply and divide.
  4. Sense check: more servings should need more cups.

A flipped side, such as cups/servings = servings/cups, gives an answer that is wildly too big or too small. Also, do not add to scale: if servings go up by 4, cups do not go up by 4.

example.prompt: On a map, 1/2 inch represents 12 miles. Two cities are 3 3/4 inches apart on the map. What is the actual distance?
steps: x = 45 ÷ 0.5 = 90. Sense check: 1 inch is 24 miles, so about 4 inches is a bit under 96 miles.

check.prompt: A cookie recipe uses 3/4 cup of sugar to make 18 cookies. How many cups of sugar are needed to make 60 cookies?

mistakes.why: Your proportion has one side flipped: 0.75/18 = 60/x (cups/cookies = cookies/cups). Keep the labels in the same positions: 0.75/18 = x/60.
You added: the cookies went up by 42, so you added 42 to 3/4 cup. Recipes scale by multiplying. Set up 0.75/18 = x/60 and cross multiply.

check.explain:
Labels: cups/cookies = cups/cookies.

0.75/18 = x/60

Cross multiply: 18x = 0.75 × 60 = 45.

x = 45 ÷ 18 = 2.5 cups (2 1/2 cups).

Sense check: 60 cookies is a little more than 3 batches of 18, and 3 × 3/4 = 2 1/4 cups, so 2 1/2 is reasonable.

screens.title: Fractions, Decimals, and Percents
screens.html:
Percent means “out of 100.” 45% means 45 out of 100, or 45/100, or 0.45.

ChangeHowExample
Percent → decimalMove the point 2 places left7% = 0.07; 125% = 1.25
Decimal → percentMove the point 2 places right0.6 = 60%; 0.045 = 4.5%
Fraction → percentDivide top by bottom, then move right3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%

A percent over 100% is a decimal greater than 1. A percent under 1% is a decimal less than 0.01: 0.5% = 0.005.

example.prompt: Write 3/5 as a percent, and write 0.4% as a decimal.

check.prompt:
Choose the value that makes each statement true.

0.08 = {{0}}

7/20 = {{1}}

150% = {{2}} (as a decimal)

why: You moved the decimal point only one place. Decimal to percent moves it two places right: 0.08 → 8%.
You treated 0.08 like 0.8. Move the point two places right: 0.08 = 8%. (80% would be 0.80.)
7 ÷ 20 = 0.35 is the decimal. To write it as a percent, move the point two places right: 35%. Adding a percent sign to 0.35 makes a number 100 times too small.
You wrote the digits 7 and 20 side by side. A fraction means divide: 7 ÷ 20 = 0.35 = 35%.
You moved the decimal point only one place. Percent to decimal moves it two places left: 150% → 1.50.
You moved the decimal point three places. 150% → 1.50 (two places left). A percent over 100% is more than 1.

check.hint: Decimal to percent: two places right. Percent to decimal: two places left. Fraction: divide first.
check.explain:
0.08 → move two places right → 8%.

7/20 = 7 ÷ 20 = 0.35 → 35%.

150% → move two places left → 1.5.

screens.title: The Three Percent Questions
screens.html:
Almost every percent question uses one relationship:

part = percent × whole   (or part/whole = percent/100)

  • Find the part: multiply. What is 15% of 60? 0.15 × 60 = 9.
  • Find the percent: divide part by whole. 27 is what percent of 36? 27 ÷ 36 = 0.75 = 75%.
  • Find the whole: divide part by percent. 18 is 40% of what number? 18 ÷ 0.40 = 45.

In word problems, “of” usually points to the whole and “is” usually points to the part. Sense check: if the percent is under 100%, the whole is bigger than the part.

example.prompt: A worker has paid $630 of his $1,800 annual union dues so far. What percent has he paid?

mistakes.why: You multiplied 0.60 × 24. Here 24 is the part, and the whole is missing, so divide: 24 ÷ 0.60 = 40.
You added 60% of 24 to 24 (24 × 1.6). The 24 is the part; the whole is 24 ÷ 0.60 = 40.

check.hint: Write part = percent × whole and fill in what you know.
check.explain:
part = percent × whole: 24 = 0.60 × whole.

whole = 24 ÷ 0.60 = 40.

Check: 60% of 40 = 0.6 × 40 = 24. Sense check: 24 is only part of the number, so the number must be bigger than 24.

screens.title: Discounts, Sales Tax, and Tips
screens.html:
• A discount is subtracted. Shortcut: multiply by (1 − rate). 30% off means you pay 70%: price × 0.70.
  • Sales tax and tips are added. Shortcut: multiply by (1 + rate). 6% tax means you pay 106%: price × 1.06.

When there is more than one percent, apply them one at a time, each to the price at that moment. Tax is figured on the sale price, after discounts.

Mental math: 10% means move the decimal point one place left. For a $46.00 bill: 10% = $4.60, 5% = $2.30, so 15% = $6.90 and 20% = $9.20.

example.prompt: A jacket costs $85. It is 30% off, and 6% sales tax is charged on the sale price. What is the total?

check.prompt: A $220 bicycle is on sale for 35% off. What is the sale price?

mistakes.why: $77 is the discount (0.35 × $220), the amount you save. The sale price is what you pay: $220 − $77 = $143.
You added 35% instead of subtracting it ($220 × 1.35). A discount lowers the price: $220 × 0.65 = $143.

check.hint: 35% off means you pay what percent of the price?
check.explain:
Discount: 0.35 × $220 = $77.

Sale price: $220 − $77 = $143.

Shortcut: you pay 65%, and 0.65 × $220 = $143.

The most common mistake is stopping at $77, which is the discount, not the price.

screens.title: Percent Change
screens.html:
percent change = (new − original) ÷ original, then write the decimal as a percent.

  • The base is always the original, the value you started with.
  • A positive result is an increase; a negative result is a decrease.

Dividing by the new value is the most common trap. If a price goes from $2.50 to $2.75, the change is $0.25 and the increase is 0.25 ÷ 2.50 = 10%, not 0.25 ÷ 2.75 ≈ 9.1%.

example.prompt: A shirt was marked down from $40 to $34. What is the percent decrease?

check.prompt: A town's population grew from 8,000 to 9,200. What was the percent increase?

mistakes.why: You divided by the new population (1,200 ÷ 9,200 ≈ 13%). Percent change divides by the original: 1,200 ÷ 8,000 = 15%.
115% is the new population as a percent of the old one (9,200 ÷ 8,000). The increase is 115% − 100% = 15%.
1,200 is the change in people, not a percent. Divide it by the original population: 1,200 ÷ 8,000 = 0.15 = 15%.

check.hint: Find the change, then divide by the starting population.

screens.title: Working Backward and Percents in a Row
screens.html:
Working backward. If you know a price after a percent change, divide by the multiplier to get the original.

  • After 25% off, the sale price is 75% of the original: original = sale price ÷ 0.75.
  • After a 4% raise, new pay is 104% of the old pay: old pay = new pay ÷ 1.04.

Do not add the percent back on. The percent was taken from the original, not from the new amount.

Percents in a row do not simply add or cancel. $100 up 20% is $120; then down 20% is $120 × 0.80 = $96, not $100. Twenty percent off and then an extra 10% off is $100 × 0.80 × 0.90 = $72, which is 28% off, not 30%.

example.prompt: After a 25% discount, a coat costs $66. What was the original price?
steps: The sale price is 75% of the original: 0.75 × original = $66.

check.prompt: After a 4% raise, Tanya earns $20.80 per hour. What was her hourly pay before the raise?
why: You subtracted 4% of the new pay ($20.80 − $0.83). The raise was 4% of the old pay, so divide: $20.80 ÷ 1.04 = $20.00.
You subtracted 4 dollars instead of 4 percent. A 4% raise on about $20 is about 80 cents.
You added another 4% ($20.80 × 1.04). The old pay must be less than the new pay.
check.hint: The new pay is 104% of the old pay.
check.explain:
New pay = 1.04 × old pay, so 1.04 × old pay = $20.80.

old pay = 20.80 ÷ 1.04 = $20.00.

Check: 4% of $20.00 is $0.80, and $20.00 + $0.80 = $20.80.

The tempting answer $19.97 takes 4% of the new pay; the raise was figured on the old pay.

screens.title: Simple Interest
screens.html:
Interest is the extra money paid for using money: you pay it on a loan, and you earn it on savings. Simple interest uses this formula from the GED formula sheet:

I = Prt   I = interest, P = principal (starting amount), r = yearly rate as a decimal, t = time in years

  • Change months to years by dividing by 12: 30 months = 2.5 years; 8 months = 2/3 year.
  • Change the rate to a decimal: 4.5% = 0.045.
  • The total paid back, or the account balance, is P + I.

Read the last sentence: “How much interest?” wants I. “How much in all?” wants P + I.

example.prompt: Tasha borrows $3,000 for a used car at 7% simple interest per year for 2 years. How much does she pay back in all?

check.prompt: Luis puts $5,000 in a savings account that earns 2.5% simple interest per year. He makes no other deposits or withdrawals. How much is in the account after 4 years?

mistakes.why: $500 is the interest. The question asks how much is in the account: $5,000 + $500 = $5,500.
You used 0.25 for 2.5%. Move the point two places left: 2.5% = 0.025. Then I = 5,000 × 0.025 × 4 = $500.
That is the balance after only 1 year. Use t = 4: I = 5,000 × 0.025 × 4 = $500.

check.hint: Find I = Prt first. Does the question want the interest or the total?
check.explain:
I = Prt = 5,000 × 0.025 × 4.

5,000 × 0.025 = 125 per year; 125 × 4 = $500.

Total in the account: $5,000 + $500 = $5,500.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• A ratio compares two quantities in the order of the words. Simplify like a fraction. A ratio a:b has a + b parts in all.
  • To split a total in a ratio: add the parts, divide the total by that sum, then multiply.
  • A unit rate is the amount for one unit; divide to find it. The lower unit price is the better buy. d = rt.
  • Proportions: label the units in matching positions, cross multiply, divide, and sense check.
  • Percent means “out of 100.” Move the decimal point two places to switch between percents and decimals.
  • part = percent × whole. Multiply to find the part; divide to find the percent or the whole.
  • Discount: × (1 − rate). Tax or tip: × (1 + rate). Several percents: one at a time.
  • Percent change = (new − original) ÷ original. To work backward, divide by the multiplier.
  • Simple interest: I = Prt with t in years. The total is P + I.

Next: Practice Set A. If you score under 80%, practice the same skills again with Set B. Then take the Exit Check.

items.prompt: A community center's basketball program has 36 adult volunteers and 48 youth players. What is the ratio of adult volunteers to youth players in simplest form?
why: 4:3 has the order reversed; it compares youth players to volunteers. The question names volunteers first, so 36 comes first: 36:48 = 3:4.
3:7 compares volunteers to everyone in the program (36:84). The question asks for volunteers to players, which is part to part: 36:48.
4:7 compares youth players to everyone in the program (48:84). The question asks for volunteers to players: 36:48 = 3:4.
items.hint: Write the numbers in the same order as the words, then divide both by their greatest common factor.
items.explain:
Write the ratio in the order the question asks: volunteers to players = 36:48.

The greatest common factor of 36 and 48 is 12.

36 ÷ 12 = 3 and 48 ÷ 12 = 4, so the ratio is 3:4.

4:3 has the order reversed (players to volunteers). 3:7 compares volunteers to everyone in the program (36:84), and 4:7 compares players to everyone (48:84). Neither is volunteers to players.

items.prompt:
A 12-pack of sparkling water costs $5.64. What is the price per can?

Enter the amount in dollars.

mistakes.why: You divided cans by dollars (12 ÷ 5.64 ≈ 2.13), which is cans per dollar. “Price per can” means dollars ÷ cans: 5.64 ÷ 12 = 0.47.
You multiplied 5.64 × 12. The price of one can must be less than the price of the whole pack, so divide: 5.64 ÷ 12 = 0.47.

items.hint: “Price per can” means dollars divided by cans.
items.explain:
Price per can = dollars ÷ cans.

$5.64 ÷ 12 = $0.47 per can.

Check: 12 × $0.47 = $5.64.

If you got about 2.13, you divided the wrong way: that is cans per dollar.

items.prompt:
Keisha's restaurant bill is $55.00. She wants to leave an 18% tip. How much is the tip?

Enter the amount in dollars.

mistakes.why: You used 1.8 for 18%. Move the decimal point two places left: 18% = 0.18, and 0.18 × $55 = $9.90. A tip larger than the bill should be a red flag.
$64.90 is the bill plus the tip. The question asks only for the tip: 0.18 × $55.00 = $9.90.

items.hint: Change 18% to a decimal, then multiply by the bill.
items.explain:
Change the percent to a decimal: 18% = 0.18

Multiply: 0.18 × $55.00 = $9.90

Check with benchmarks: 10% of $55 is $5.50, 20% is $11.00, so 18% should be a little less than $11. $9.90 fits.

A common mistake is to use 1.8 instead of 0.18, which gives $99, far more than the bill itself.

items.skill: Splitting a total in a ratio
items.prompt: A trail mix recipe uses peanuts and raisins in a ratio of 3:2 by weight. Jordan makes 40 ounces of trail mix. How many ounces of peanuts are in it?

mistakes.why: 16 ounces is the raisins (2 parts × 8). Peanuts are the 3 parts: 3 × 8 = 24.
You divided 40 by 2 and multiplied by 3, as if the 40 ounces were only the raisins. 40 ounces is the whole mix, which is 3 + 2 = 5 parts.
That splits the mix evenly. A 3:2 ratio means peanuts are 3 of the 5 equal parts: 3 × 8 = 24.

items.hint: Add the parts of the ratio to find how many equal parts are in the 40 ounces.
items.explain:
Total parts: 3 + 2 = 5.

One part: 40 ÷ 5 = 8 ounces.

items.prompt: A cyclist rides 27 miles in 1.5 hours. At the same average speed, how many minutes will it take her to ride 45 miles?

notes:
Week 2 Study Sheet: Ratios, Rates, Proportions, and Percents

Ratios and Rates

  • Ratio a:b = a to b = a/b. Order matches the words.
  • Simplify: divide both terms by the GCF. 36:48 = 3:4.
  • a:b has a + b parts. First part = a/(a + b) of the whole.
  • Split a total: total ÷ (a + b) = one part; multiply.
  • Unit rate = first quantity ÷ second (“per” means divide).
  • Unit price = price ÷ units. Lower unit price = better buy.
  • d = rt; r = d ÷ t; t = d ÷ r. Minutes ÷ 60 = hours.

Proportions

  • Label units first: miles/inches = miles/inches.
  • If a/b = c/d, then a × d = b × c.
  • Divide to get x alone.
  • Scale by multiplying, never by adding.
  • Sense check: bigger situation, bigger answer.

Example: 1.5/6 = x/10 → 6x = 15 → x = 2.5

Percents

  • Percent → decimal: point 2 left (7% = 0.07; 0.5% = 0.005).
  • Decimal → percent: point 2 right (0.6 = 60%).
  • part = percent × whole
  • Percent = part ÷ whole. Whole = part ÷ percent.
  • Discount: × (1 − rate). Tax or tip: × (1 + rate).
  • Several percents: one at a time, on the current price.

Change, Working Backward, Interest

  • Percent change = (new − original) ÷ original.
  • Working backward: after 25% off, original = sale price ÷ 0.75.
  • Simple interest: I = Prt (r as a decimal, t in years).
  • Months ÷ 12 = years. Total = P + I.

Example: $2,400 at 4.5% for 3 years: I = 2,400 × 0.045 × 3 = $324; total $2,724
